title: CTV Attribution Playbook: A Guide to Performance Campaign Success

paragraphs.text: Meta description: How to set up CTV attribution, measure it honestly, and prove performance — a practical playbook for brands buying Connected TV.
Target keyword: CTV attribution

Connected TV is the fastest-growing line item in most performance budgets, and it's also the one most marketers trust the least — not because it doesn't work, but because it's measured with tools built for a different channel. This playbook lays out how CTV attribution actually functions, where it breaks down, and how to set up a campaign so the credit lands where the performance happened.
Why CTV attribution is a different problem

Search and social attribution is click-based: a user taps an ad, an MMP (mobile measurement partner) logs a click ID, and when that same device installs an app or converts, the click gets the credit. CTV doesn't have a click. A living-room ad plays on a shared household screen, and the "signal" your MMP has to work with is a household IP address and device user agent — not a click ID tied to one person's phone. That single difference cascades into everything else:

Attribution is probabilistic, not deterministic. The MMP is matching a TV impression to a mobile install by IP and user agent proximity, not a 1:1 click. Shorter windows miss real conversions; windows that are too generous can over-match.
Attribution windows vary by MMP — some platforms default to short lookback windows built for click attribution, which quietly discount CTV before the analysis even starts.

IPv4 vs. IPv6 support is inconsistent. Not every MMP handles both, and that gap alone can silently drop a meaningful share of legitimate CTV-driven installs, particularly on OEM inventory that has moved to IPv6.

CTV sits at the bottom of most attribution waterfalls. When a user sees a CTV ad, picks up their phone later, and converts through a paid search or affiliate click, the last click wins by default — even though the TV ad is what put the brand in front of them in the first place. We go deeper on this in The Last-Click Blind Spot.
Setting up attribution correctly, before you launch
Confirm your MMP passes both IP and user agent on every impression, not just clicks. This is the household-to-device match that makes CTV attribution possible at all.

Set an attribution window that reflects real household behavior, not a default built for mobile. A 24–72 hour window is a reasonable performance-channel starting point, but validate it against your own conversion curve rather than accepting the platform default.
Check IPv4/IPv6 support before you scale spend. Ask your MMP directly whether CTV impressions on IPv6 networks are captured — this is a common, quiet source of under-attribution.

Use a dedicated CTV link or pixel, not your mobile click URL. Blending CTV impressions into a generic mobile link makes it functionally impossible to separate CTV-driven performance from every other channel later.

Pressure-test the MMP's attribution priority (waterfall) settings. Ask specifically how the platform ranks a CTV impression against a later paid search or affiliate click — and whether that ranking can be adjusted so CTV isn't automatically deprioritized. Equal attribution windows and priority settings are becoming standard requests for exactly this reason, as outlined in our guide to equal attribution priority windows.
Incrementality is your ground truth

Attribution tells you what a platform is credited. Incrementality tells you what actually happened. Running a structured incrementality test — holdout groups, geo splits, or PSA-based controls — alongside your attribution data is the only way to know whether CTV is truly driving conversions or simply reaching people who would have converted anyway.

In one recent incrementality readout, a CTV campaign delivered lift more than 10x the client's target benchmark, a gap that attribution data alone never would have revealed. We break down how to structure these tests in The CTV Test Framework.
A practical checklist
MMP passes IP + user agent on every CTV impression
Attribution window validated against real conversion timing, not left at default
IPv4/IPv6 support confirmed
Dedicated CTV tracking link, separate from mobile click URLs
Attribution priority/waterfall settings reviewed and adjusted where possible
An incrementality test scheduled within the first 60–90 days
FAQ

Is CTV attribution the same as mobile attribution? No. Mobile attribution is click-based and deterministic. CTV attribution is impression-based and probabilistic, matched via household IP and device user agent rather than a click ID.

Why does CTV often look like it's underperforming in reporting? Because most attribution systems were built for click-based channels and rank CTV impressions below last-click channels like paid search or affiliates in the attribution waterfall — even when the CTV ad drove the original intent.

What's the single highest-leverage fix? Pairing correct MMP setup (IP/UA passback, validated windows, IPv6 support) with a real incrementality test. Attribution and incrementality answer different questions, and you need both.

title: CTV Attribution That Works: How to Capture the Conversions Last Click Misses

paragraphs.text: Meta description: Most CTV conversions never make it into a dashboard. Here's the technical setup — attribution windows, MMP configuration, and priority settings — that gets CTV the credit it earns.
Target keyword: CTV attribution setup

Every performance marketer has seen it: a CTV campaign that clearly moved the business, next to a dashboard that says it barely converted. The gap isn't performance — it's configuration. Here's the technical setup that closes it.
Start with the match, not the metric

CTV attribution isn't measuring a click; it's inferring a connection between a household TV impression and a mobile conversion, using IP address and device user agent as the bridge. Get that match wrong, or lose part of it, and every downstream metric is compromised before you've looked at a single report.
A few setup details determine whether that match works:

IP + user agent passback on impressions, not just clicks. Confirm your OEM/publisher-side integration and your MMP are both configured to log this on every served impression. This sounds basic, and it's the single most common gap we see.

IPv6 coverage. A growing share of connected TV traffic runs on IPv6, and not every MMP matches it with the same fidelity as IPv4. If your MMP can't confirm IPv6 handling, ask — this is a real source of silently lost attribution, not an edge case.

Cross-device logic. Some MMPs fire duplicate conversion events when a household has more than one device on the same network, inflating impression counts without inflating real performance. Ask your MMP directly how they de-duplicate within a household.
Attribution windows: the setting nobody checks

Most MMPs ship with attribution windows tuned for click-based channels — short, because a click implies immediate intent. CTV intent doesn't move that fast. Someone sees a masthead ad on their living room TV, and the resulting app open or purchase might happen an hour later on their phone, or the next day.

A window that's too short doesn't make CTV "less effective" — it makes CTV invisible in the data. Test windows in the 24–72 hour range against your own conversion curve rather than accepting a default built for a faster-moving channel, and revisit the setting as your data matures.
Attribution priority: the setting that actually decides who gets credit

This is the one most teams never touch, and it's the one that matters most. Every MMP ranks channels in a priority order — a "waterfall" — to decide who gets credit when a user's journey touches more than one source. In most default configurations, deterministic clicks (paid search, affiliate, app store search ads) outrank probabilistic CTV impressions automatically, regardless of sequence or actual influence. That means a user who saw your CTV ad Tuesday night and searched your brand name Wednesday morning gets attributed entirely to paid search — not because search did the work, but because search fired a click and CTV didn't.
Ask your MMP whether:
CTV impressions can be weighted equally with — not automatically below — later clicks within a defined window
Priority rules can be customized per channel rather than left at platform default
You can view assisted, not just last-touch, attribution for CTV specifically

Feedmob’s guide to equal attribution settings is a useful reference for how this is implemented across platforms like AppsFlyer, Adjust, and Singular — the mechanics vary by MMP, but the principle is the same everywhere: don't let a default ranking decide your channel mix for you.
Reporting: separate CTV from everything else

Use a CTV-specific tracking link rather than folding CTV impressions into a general mobile URL. Without that separation, you can't isolate CTV performance later, you can't run a clean incrementality test against it, and you can't have an honest conversation with your team about what the channel is actually doing.
What good CTV attribution setup looks like in practice
Dedicated CTV link/pixel, confirmed IP + UA passback on every impression
IPv6 coverage confirmed with your MMP directly
Attribution window tested and set against real data, not platform default
Attribution priority reviewed — CTV weighted fairly, not automatically deprioritized
Assisted-conversion reporting available for CTV specifically
Incrementality testing scheduled to validate what attribution can't fully capture (see The CTV Test Framework)
FAQ

Why does my MMP show almost no CTV conversions even though sales are up? Most likely one of three things: the attribution window is too short for how long CTV-driven consideration actually takes, IP/UA passback isn't fully configured, or your MMP's default priority settings are giving credit to a later click instead of the CTV impression that started the journey.

What's an "equal attribution priority window"? A setting some MMPs support that lets CTV impressions compete fairly with clicks from other channels for conversion credit within a set window, instead of being automatically ranked last. See FeedMob’s guide to equal attribution windows.

How do I know if my attribution window is too short? Look at the time gap between CTV impression and conversion for the installs you do capture. If a meaningful share lands near the edge of your window, you're likely truncating real conversions that fall just outside it.

title: The Last-Click Blind Spot: How CTV Drives Conversions That Other Channels Take Credit For

paragraphs.text: Meta description: Last-click attribution rewards whichever channel touches a conversion last — not whichever channel actually drove it. Here's why CTV falls into what growth marketers call the "last-click valley of death," and how to see past it.
Target keyword: last-click attribution CTV

Nick Fairbairn, VP of Growth Marketing at Chime, gave this problem a name that's stuck in performance marketing circles: the last-click valley of death. It describes what happens when a channel does the real work of creating demand, only for a different channel — usually paid search or an affiliate — to sweep in at the final step and take the credit for a conversion that was already decided. CTV lives in that valley more than almost any other channel.
The waterfall, and why it works against CTV

Picture the media waterfall first — the one buyers see in a sales deck. Direct brand sales sit at the top: the most expensive, highest-quality inventory, sold directly by the publisher. Right after that tier, before the inventory drops into the open market, sits the highest-value performance placement — full-screen, first-look impressions with premium attention, before a viewer has seen four or five other ads competing for the same few seconds. That's a valuable place to buy.

Now picture a second waterfall — the attribution waterfall — and this one works in the opposite direction. Most MMPs rank channels by how they touch a conversion, not by how much they actually influenced it. A deterministic click — from paid search, an app store ad, or an affiliate link — outranks a probabilistic CTV impression automatically, every time, regardless of which one actually happened first or did more to move the user. So the sequence plays out like this:
A user sees your ad on the biggest screen in their home — full attention, no scroll, no skip.
They pick up their phone later and search your brand name, or click a retargeting ad, or land through an affiliate link they'd already bookmarked.
The last click wins the attribution model. Paid search, or the affiliate, gets 100% of the credit.
CTV — the channel that actually created the intent — shows up in the dashboard as if it did nothing.
That's the last-click valley of death: real influence, systematically miscredited to whichever channel happened to close the loop.
What this looks like as a real result

In a recent incrementality test on a CTV campaign, the relative lift target was 5–10% — a reasonable, conservative benchmark. The actual result was a 110% lift: more than ten times the target, measured by comparing exposed and unexposed audiences directly rather than relying on last-click attribution alone. That's the size of the gap between what attribution reports and what CTV does. Attribution data alone would have shown a channel that looked flat. The incrementality test showed a channel that was quietly driving the majority of new business.

This is consistent with what independent researchers have found industry-wide: last-click models systematically undervalue upper- and mid-funnel channels in favor of whichever touchpoint happens to close last, and CTV is disproportionately affected because it can't fire a deterministic click at all. See AdTaxi's analysis of proving CTV performance without last-click attribution and ATTN Agency's guide to moving CTV measurement beyond last-click for more on how this plays out across DTC and performance brands broadly.
Getting out of the valley
You don't fix a structural measurement bias by hoping the dashboard improves. You fix it by changing what you measure:

Run incrementality tests, not just attribution reports. Attribution tells you who touched the conversion last. Incrementality tells you whether the conversion would have happened without the ad at all. Both matter; only one tells you the truth about CTV specifically. See The CTV Test Framework for how to structure one.
Review assisted conversions, not just last-touch. Most MMPs can show you this view — it's usually just never turned on by default.

Price the channel so incentives are aligned, not stacked against honest measurement. A CPM model rewards accurate attribution instead of penalizing the buyer for fixing it, as covered in The CTV Attribution Playbook.

Treat the media waterfall and the attribution waterfall as two separate conversations. Buying high in the media waterfall gets you premium attention. Fixing the attribution waterfall is what gets that attention counted.
FAQ

What is the "last-click valley of death"? A phrase popularized by Nick Fairbairn, VP of Growth Marketing at Chime, describing how last-click attribution models give conversion credit to whichever channel touches a customer journey last — even when that channel did little to create the original intent. Upper-funnel, high-attention channels like CTV are the most common casualties.

Why is CTV especially vulnerable to this? CTV impressions are impression-based and probabilistic, not click-based. Most attribution waterfalls rank deterministic clicks above probabilistic impressions by default, so a CTV ad that starts the journey routinely loses the conversion credit to whatever channel closes it — usually paid search or an affiliate.

How do you prove CTV is working if attribution understates it? Run a controlled incrementality test — holdout or exposed-vs-unexposed groups — alongside attribution reporting. Incrementality measures actual causal lift, independent of which channel the attribution model happens to credit.

title: The CTV Test Framework: A Practical Guide to Measuring Incremental Lift

paragraphs.text: Meta description: A step-by-step framework for structuring a CTV incrementality test — from holdout design to statistical significance — built for AdOps and performance marketing teams running Connected TV campaigns.
Target keyword: CTV incrementality test

Attribution tells you what got credited. Only a well-built incrementality test tells you what actually happened. This framework is written for AdOps and performance marketing teams who need to stand up a CTV test that produces a defensible answer — not just a nice-looking chart.
Start with the right question

Before choosing a methodology, define what "incremental" means for this specific campaign: incremental installs, incremental enrollments, incremental revenue, or incremental activity within an existing user base. The test design changes depending on the answer, and skipping this step is the most common reason a test produces an ambiguous result.
Choose a methodology that fits your scale and timeline

PSA-based holdouts (public service announcement swaps). A portion of the audience that would otherwise see your ad instead sees a neutral PSA, creating a clean control group within the same media environment. This is a strong default for CTV specifically because it controls for the same inventory, timing, and viewing context — the only variable that changes is whether the brand's ad or a neutral one was shown.

Geo/DMA holdouts. Entire markets are held out from CTV delivery while others receive full exposure, then performance is compared market-to-market. This works well when you have enough geographic scale to hold out statistically meaningful markets without starving the test of volume, and it's often easier to stand up quickly than a PSA swap.

Audience holdouts. A randomized subset of your addressable audience is excluded from delivery. This requires tighter frequency-capping discipline than geo holdouts, because any overlap between the test and control groups at the household level will quietly erode your result — see the IP frequency-capping note below.

For a broader look at how these approaches compare, look at MarTech's guide to running a CTV incrementality test — the specific tradeoffs are consistent across the industry, independent of which DSP or MMP is running the test.
Design the test to actually hold up

Set frequency caps at the IP level, not just the device level, so a single household can't land in both the test and control groups. This is the most common silent failure point in CTV incrementality tests — a household that's supposed to be "unexposed" but still sees the ad through a second device breaks the comparison without anyone noticing until the results come back muddy.

Size the test to your expected effect, not your budget. A small lift on a small sample won't clear statistical significance, and a test that can't reach significance isn't a test — it's a guess with a chart attached. Set expectations on required sample size and runtime before launch, not after the data disappoints.
Hold the creative and flighting constant between test and control cells (outside of the intentional PSA swap) so the only variable that changed is exposure.

Give the test enough runtime to mature. Some conversion events — like a funded direct deposit versus an initial signup — take longer to mature than an install event. Reporting a test result before downstream metrics have had time to catch up will understate the true lift.

Validate your control group's balance before reading results. Confirm test and control cohorts are demographically and behaviorally comparable going in; an imbalanced control group will produce a lift number that looks real and isn't.
Reading the result honestly

Report against the pre-defined success benchmark, not a benchmark chosen after seeing the data. Real CTV incrementality results can be dramatic — lift well beyond initial targets is not unusual for a channel that's been systematically under-credited by attribution up to this point (see The Last-Click Blind Spot) — but a result that looks "too good" is exactly when test hygiene matters most. Check for control group contamination, exposure overlap, and seasonality effects before presenting a headline number.
Walk before you run

A practical sequencing that works well for CTV specifically: validate the channel can perform at all with a straightforward attribution-based test first, then layer in a structured incrementality test once there's enough delivery volume to power a statistically sound result, then use that result to inform scaled budget decisions. Trying to run a full DMA holdout on day one of a new campaign, before delivery has stabilized, is a common way to burn a test on noisy early data.
Test framework checklist
Success metric defined before launch (installs, enrollments, revenue — pick one)
Methodology chosen to fit scale: PSA swap, geo/DMA holdout, or audience holdout
IP-level frequency capping in place to prevent test/control overlap
Sample size and runtime set against expected effect size, not against budget
Creative and flighting held constant outside the intentional test variable
Control group balance validated pre-read
Result reported against pre-defined benchmark, with contamination checks before presenting
FAQ

What's the difference between attribution and incrementality? Attribution assigns credit to a touchpoint based on a model's rules. Incrementality measures whether a conversion would have happened anyway, by comparing exposed and unexposed groups. They answer different questions, and a channel can look weak in attribution while proving strong in incrementality — this is common with CTV specifically.

How long should a CTV incrementality test run? Long enough for your slowest-maturing conversion event to fully develop — for a fast event like an app install, that may be days; for a metric like a funded account or completed transaction, it can be weeks. Reading results before the metric has matured will understate real lift.

What's the most common reason a CTV incrementality test fails? Overlap between test and control groups at the household level, usually from frequency capping that's set at the device level instead of the IP level, letting a "control" household still see the ad through a second screen.

title: Creatives That Perform: CTV Creative Best Practices

paragraphs.text: Meta description: What actually performs on the biggest screen in the house — CTA design, video specs, creative refresh cadence, and production workflow best practices for Connected TV campaigns.
Target keyword: CTV creative best practices

CTV is a full-screen, sound-on, first-look format — closer to a 15-second brand film than a banner ad. What performs there follows different rules than what performs on a phone screen, and getting the format right is often the difference between a campaign that scales and one that plateaus. These are the best practices we've validated running performance creative across CTV inventory over the past year.
Design the CTA for a remote, not a finger

A CTV viewer can't tap. Most smart TV interfaces route a CTA click into a secondary action — playing a video, opening an app-store-style overlay — rather than a direct web navigation, so the CTA needs to work with that behavior rather than against it. Two practices matter most:

Skip the QR code as your primary CTA. QR codes ask a viewer to stop what they're doing, pick up a second device, and manually scan a screen from across the room — friction that a living-room format doesn't reward. A clear, simple instruction ("Download Now" or "Sign Up Now") that triggers an on-screen action consistently outperforms a QR-first approach.

Write for the second screen explicitly. If the intended action ultimately happens on a phone, say so — plainly and early in the creative, not as a small footer line. Clarity beats cleverness in a format where the viewer is often multitasking.

Always include app store badges in the creative. It sounds like a small detail, but a multi-device world needs multi-device clarity when it comes to the ask. Whether the badges sit on the video end card or a static unit, they tell the viewer exactly what to do next — open the App Store, open Google Play, no guessing. The same logic applies when the destination is a mobile website rather than an app: give the CTA a clear, explicit direction ("Go to yourwebsite.com to sign up today"), not just a generic "Learn More." A CTV viewer is already relying on a second screen to act — don't make them guess what that action is.
Faces perform

Across performance campaigns, creative featuring real human faces — UGC-style talent, actors, or well-produced AI-generated people — has consistently outperformed abstract or purely graphic treatments. A CTV ad is playing in someone's living room; a format that feels human tends to hold attention better than one that feels like a banner blown up to television size.
Get the technical spec right the first time
CTV creative rejections are almost always avoidable, and they cost campaign days that performance budgets don't have. The recurring issues:
Exact duration. Almost all CTV inventory requires precisely 15- or 30-second videos — not "close to." A video that's a second long or short will bounce at review.

Variable bitrate, not constant bitrate, HD transcoding. Constant bitrate encoding is a common cause of delivery failures on programmatic CTV routes. Confirm that your production vendor or in-house team is exporting variable bitrate by default.
File size discipline. Keep video files well under platform limits (commonly 25–50MB, tightening toward the lower end is safer) to avoid slow delivery or outright rejection.

Naming conventions that hold up at scale. Once a campaign is running multiple line items, advertiser- and partner-based naming isn't a nice-to-have — it's what keeps spend and performance data attributable to the right creative later.
Run more than one creative

Two to three creative variants, tested against each other from the start, is a reasonable minimum for any CTV campaign meant to scale. A single-creative campaign has no way to isolate whether a performance dip is fatigue, format fit, or something else entirely. Build refresh into the plan from day one rather than reacting to fatigue after it's already cost performance — a general cadence of refreshing creative on a regular seasonal or promotional rhythm keeps delivery healthy longer than a "set it and forget it" approach.
Respect the review clock

CTV creative review isn't instant — most platforms require a standard lead time (commonly 48 hours to two business days) ahead of launch, with corporate-level review adding time for certain partners. Build that lead time into the campaign plan itself, not as a scramble before go-live. Minor optimizations post-launch — swapping a static asset, adjusting copy — are typically much faster than net-new creative submissions, so plan major creative changes with the full review window in mind.
Compliance is not optional, and it's not slow if you plan for it

Disclaimers, legal fine print, and brand-safety review should be resolved before a creative enters the submission queue, not during it. This is especially true for regulated categories (fintech, crypto) and for markets with strict advertising-to-minors guidelines — creative should never feature imagery or messaging that implies a youth audience, regardless of category.
Creative checklist
CTA designed for remote/second-screen behavior, not a tap
QR code is not the primary call to action
Real human faces considered, especially for fintech/consumer categories
Exact duration confirmed (15s or 30s, not approximate)
Variable bitrate HD export confirmed with your production pipeline
File size within platform limits
Consistent naming convention applied across line items
2–3 creative variants live from launch
Refresh cadence planned, not reactive
Submission timed to the platform's review window, with compliance cleared in advance
FAQ

Why do QR codes underperform on CTV? Because they require a viewer to interrupt what they're doing, retrieve a second device, and manually scan a screen from a distance — friction that a full-screen, sound-on living-room format doesn't reward compared to a direct, simple on-screen instruction.

How many creative variants should a CTV campaign launch with? Two to three is a reasonable minimum, giving you enough signal to A/B test and isolate performance issues without spreading budget too thin to reach significance on any one variant.

What's the most common reason CTV creative gets rejected? Technical spec misses — most often incorrect video duration or constant-bitrate encoding where variable bitrate HD is required — rather than content or compliance issues.

title: IPv4 vs. IPv6 on CTV: An IP 101 for Performance Marketers

paragraphs.text: Every other article in this series mentions IP address matching as the foundation of CTV attribution. This is the primer behind that reference — what an IP address actually is, why CTV depends on it so heavily, and why IPv4 and IPv6 behave differently enough to change what your reporting shows.
Why CTV attribution starts with an IP address at all

Mobile and search attribution is click-based: a user taps an ad, the click carries an ID, and that ID gets matched to the resulting install or purchase. A living-room CTV ad has no click to carry. So the industry uses the next best signal — the household's shared internet connection. Every device on a home network, whether it's the smart TV, a laptop, or a phone, connects through the same public IP address issued by the internet service provider. When a CTV ad is served, the platform logs that IP alongside the impression; when someone in that household later converts on a phone or web browser, the MMP looks for a matching IP within a defined time window and credits the CTV impression. That's the entire mechanism — no click required, because the household's IP is standing in for one.
IPv4, in plain English

IPv4 is the addressing system the internet has used since the 1980s. It's built on a 32-bit format, which caps the total number of possible addresses at roughly 4.3 billion — a number the internet has long since outgrown. Two things follow from that scarcity:

Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT). Because there aren't enough IPv4 addresses to give every household its own, many ISPs — especially mobile carriers — assign one public IPv4 address to a large pool of subscribers at once. That means an IP match on IPv4 can sometimes represent dozens of unrelated households, not one, which is a real source of attribution noise on carrier networks that rely on CGNAT.

Relative stability. Where IPv4 addresses are assigned, they tend to stay assigned to the same household for a meaningful stretch of time — commonly attribution vendors see residential IPv4 addresses hold steady for months at a time. That stability is what makes IP-based matching workable at all on IPv4 — it's a slow-moving signal, which is exactly what attribution needs.
IPv6, in plain English

IPv6 was built specifically to solve IPv4's scarcity problem — its address space is effectively unlimited, so every device can get its own unique address without ever sharing through CGNAT. That's a real improvement for attribution in one specific way: it removes the "one IP, many households" problem that CGNAT creates on IPv4.
But IPv6 trades that problem for a different one. Because addresses are abundant, ISPs and devices don't need to hold onto one the way IPv4 had to:

Address rotation. Many devices use IPv6 privacy extensions that rotate the device's address on a short cycle — commonly every 24 to 72 hours — specifically to limit long-term tracking. That's a deliberate privacy feature, and it means the same TV can show up under a new address before a slower-maturing conversion event (like a funded account, not just an install) has had time to happen.

Prefix reassignment. ISPs frequently reassign the IPv6 address block a household is using, sometimes daily. A block that represented one household on Monday can represent a different household by Thursday, which is a real problem for geo-targeting precision, not just for conversion matching.

Put together: the same household can technically appear as several different "users" within a single week under IPv6, which affects frequency capping and reach reporting as much as it affects conversion attribution. For more on how this plays out at scale, IPinfo's breakdown of the IPv6 measurement challenge in CTV is a useful deeper read, and Mynt Agency's explainer on IP address matching for streaming TV covers the household identity graph approach some platforms use to compensate.
So which one is "better" for attribution? Neither, on its own

It's tempting to treat this as IPv4 good, IPv6 bad, but that's not quite right. IPv4 solves the instability problem IPv6 has, and IPv6 solves the shared-address problem IPv4 has. Neither address type is inherently more or less trustworthy — what matters is whether your MMP and DSP are built to handle both correctly:
On IPv4, the risk is over-matching — crediting a conversion to the wrong household because CGNAT put multiple homes behind one address.
On IPv6, the risk is under-matching — missing a real conversion because the household's address rotated before the match window closed.

A platform that only handles IPv4 well will quietly under-report CTV performance as more connected TV traffic shifts to IPv6 — and a meaningful share already has, with U.S. adoption above 50% and several other major markets well ahead of that. A platform that handles both, and layers in supporting signals like device user agent and household identity graphs rather than relying on IP alone, is the one that gives you a reporting number you can actually trust.
What to ask your MMP or DSP

Do you capture both IPv4 and IPv6 impressions, or only IPv4? This is the single most important question, and it's rarely asked. A platform that silently drops IPv6 traffic is silently dropping a growing share of your CTV audience.

How do you handle IPv6 address rotation within an attribution window? Ask specifically whether the platform accounts for a household's address changing mid-window, or whether a rotation simply breaks the match.
Do you supplement IP matching with other signals? Device user agent, household identity graphs, and probabilistic modeling all help offset the weaknesses of either IP version on its own.

How do you handle CGNAT on IPv4 traffic, particularly from mobile carrier networks? Ask whether the platform has any logic to avoid crediting a conversion to the wrong household when many homes share one address.
Quick-reference: IPv4 vs. IPv6 for CTV attribution
IPv4
IPv6
Address space
~4.3 billion addresses (scarce)
Effectively unlimited
Stability
Relatively stable — often months at a time
Rotates frequently — often every 24–72 hours
Main attribution risk
Over-matching via CGNAT (shared addresses)
Under-matching via address rotation and prefix reassignment
Where it shows up most
Mobile carrier / CGNAT-heavy networks
Modern ISPs, growing share of CTV device traffic
FAQ

What's the basic difference between IPv4 and IPv6? IPv4 is the older addressing system, limited to about 4.3 billion total addresses, which forces many devices to share a single address through CGNAT. IPv6 was built to solve that scarcity with a vastly larger address space, but its addresses rotate and reassign far more frequently than IPv4's do.

Why does this matter specifically for CTV, and not as much for mobile or search? Mobile and search attribution rely on a click ID, which doesn't depend on IP stability. CTV has no click, so it depends on matching a household's IP address to a later conversion — which means the behavior of that IP address, whether it's stable or constantly rotating, directly affects whether real conversions get counted.

Does IPv6 make CTV attribution worse? Not inherently — it trades one problem for another. IPv6 removes the CGNAT over-matching risk that affects IPv4, but introduces an under-matching risk from address rotation. The real issue is whether your measurement partner handles both address types well, not which one is "better."

What's the one question every CTV buyer should ask their MMP? Whether the platform captures and correctly matches both IPv4 and IPv6 impressions — not just IPv4. As IPv6 adoption climbs past 50% in the U.S. and higher elsewhere, a platform that only handles IPv4 well is under-reporting a real and growing share of CTV performance.

This article is written to be the reference point other CTV attribution articles link back to when they mention IP matching — see The CTV Attribution Playbook, CTV Attribution That Works, and The Last-Click Blind Spot for how this connects to attribution windows, waterfall priority, and incrementality testing.
